title: SQL Joins: Combining Tables
oneLiner: Real data lives in more than one table on purpose -- a JOIN is how you ask a question that spans both without duplicating data everywhere.
keyTakeaway: An INNER JOIN only keeps rows that match on both sides -- a department with zero employees would silently disappear entirely from the result. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table regardless, filling in NULLs (SQL's marker for "no value") for the side that didn't match -- which one you want depends on whether "no match" should hide the row or just leave gaps in it.
explanation:
Splitting data into multiple tables (employees in one table, departments in another) avoids repeating a department's name and location on every single employee row -- instead, each employee just stores a department_id, a foreign key pointing at the department it belongs to. That's normalization: each fact lives in exactly one place. The tradeoff is that answering "which department does Ava work in" now needs a JOIN to stitch the two tables back together for the query.

`SELECT ... FROM employees JOIN departments ON employees.department_id = departments.id` walks every employee row, finds the department row whose id matches that employee's department_id, and glues the two rows together into one wider result row -- as if, just for this one query, the two tables were combined into one. The ON clause is the matching rule; get it wrong (or forget it entirely) and you get either no rows or a cartesian product (every row of one table paired with every row of the other), both obviously broken results that are still worth recognizing on sight.

This is plain JOIN / INNER JOIN -- only pairs that actually match on both sides survive. A LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table even with no match, filling the right side's columns with NULLs instead of dropping the row -- the right choice when "no match" is itself meaningful information, not something to hide. Every department in the sample data has employees, so add one that doesn't and try it in the playground: `INSERT OR IGNORE INTO departments VALUES (4, 'Legal', 'Boston'); SELECT departments.name, employees.name FROM departments LEFT JOIN employees ON employees.department_id = departments.id;` Legal comes back once, with NULL as the employee's name.

A common LEFT JOIN bug is filtering the right table in WHERE, such as `WHERE employees.salary > 100000`. On Legal's row employees.salary is NULL, and a comparison with NULL is never true, so WHERE drops the row and the LEFT JOIN quietly behaves like an inner join. To filter the matches but still keep every department, move the condition into ON: `LEFT JOIN employees ON employees.department_id = departments.id AND employees.salary > 100000`. A WHERE condition on the left table is fine.
